title: Pulmonary talaromycosis in a non-HIV individual-A rare case report from Southern India
case_text:
A 61-year-old female presented to our OPD with the complaints of cough with scanty white expectoration for 1 week and fever with worsening of dyspnoea to mMRC grade III for 2 days. She had no recent history of travel or exposure to wild animals. She was a known case of bronchial asthma on inhaler formoterol fumarate + budesonide for the past 30 years, ABPA with bilateral upper lobe bronchiectasis and chronic respiratory failure using nocturnal oxygen at home since 2 years. Patient also had a history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections over the past 1 year, where sputum culture repeatedly grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa on three different occasions.
On arrival patient was afebrile, respiratory rate 32/min, oxygen saturation on room air was 70%, pulse rate 108/min and ABG showed hypercapnia. On examination, grade III clubbing and bilateral pitting pedal oedema were present. On auscultation, bilateral inspiratory crackles and wheeze were noted.
Routine investigation showed total leukocyte count of 12,940 cells/mm3. Rest were insignificant. Chest X-ray showed bilateral upper zone bronchiectatic changes. HRCT thorax showed multiple areas of dilated bronchi with wall thickening involving bilateral lungs, multiple small nodular opacities and interstitial thickening [Figure 1]. Serology for HIV was nonreactive. On the third day of admission, patient had worsening of symptoms requiring intensive care shift for NIV support.
Sputum culture showed heavy growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitive to colistimethate sodium. But patient had persisting symptoms despite treatment with appropriate antibiotics. Surprisingly, on the sixth day of admission sputum fungal culture in Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) showed moderate growth of penicillium species and wet mount with Lactophenol cotton blue (LCB) showed brush-like structures typical of genus Penicillium [Figure 2a and b]. Hence, patient was started on once-daily dosage of 20 mg IV lyophilized amphotericin B as per her body weight for 14 days. Followed by oral itraconazole 400 mg once daily for 10 weeks. Patient completed full course of treatment without any notable adverse effects. On 1-week follow-up patient had good resolution of symptoms with reduced oxygen requirement.
Talaromyces marneffei is initially discovered from bamboo rats (Rhizomys) in Vietnam, and the first human case was reported in 1973. The route of infection is inhalation of aerosolized fungal spores. T. marneffei is mainly lung pathogen but also disseminates to other organs via blood and lymphatics. The clinical presentation varies from mild disease showing skin lesions and lymphadenopathy to severe fatal conditions leading to respiratory failure and circulatory collapse. Our patient was immunocompetent, but her lung immunity was probably impaired due to structural damage, recurrent hospitalization and treatment with long-term systemic steroids for asthma and ABPA. Currently, the definitive diagnosis of talaromycosis is isolation of the organism in culture. Compared to other endemic dimorphic fungi, it grows more readily in standard SDA. At 25 C to 30 C, the fungus grows as a mould, producing yellow-green colonies with red diffusible pigment. Microscopically, filamentous hyphae with conidiophores and conidia are seen. At 32 C to 37 C, the fungus makes the transition from a mould to a yeast, producing tan-coloured colonies. New antigen tests, such as the Mp1P ELISA, are in development which can detect antigen in plasma and urine. Currently, none of the real-time PCR assays, serological tests and antigen tests have been validated or commercially developed for usage.
Management is same for both HIV and non-HIV individual. Treatment consists of induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. For patients with mild disease, oral itraconazole with loading dose of 200 mg thrice daily for 3 days followed by 200 mg twice daily for 12 weeks is recommended. In moderate to severe disease, induction therapy with amphotericin B at dose of 0.6-1.0 mg/kg per day for 2 weeks and followed by consolidation therapy with oral itraconazole at dose of 400 mg per day for 10 weeks is given. For HIV patients, it is recommended to continue maintenance therapy with oral itraconazole 200 mg once daily until the CD4 count is more than 100 cells/microL for at least 6 months. In conclusion, to reduce mortality, morbidity rate and to prevent relapse of this fungal infection early diagnosis followed by a full course of therapy is necessary. New research into the field for developing rapid diagnostic methods of Talaromyces marneffei is pertinent.
The authors certify that they have obtained all appropriate patient consent forms. In the form, the patient has given her consent for her images and other clinical information to be reported in the journal. The patient understands that their names and initials will not be published and that due efforts will be made to conceal their identity, but anonymity cannot be guaranteed.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Talaromycosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: pulmonary talaromycosis in an immunocompetent patient with underlying bronchiectasis
